Fast on the footsteps of the fire in San Francisco, is recorded another in Stockton, which on Wedncsdav night consumed more than half that city. It appears, by the following from the Extra Stockton Journal , that the fire is supposed to have been the work of an incendiary. The fire originated in a new and beautiful house just opened under the name of the þÿMerchants Hotel, formerly known as the Branch, and beyond a doubt was the work of an incendiary. From hc point at which it originated, the fire swept up Levee street, prostrating Montþÿgomery s tately auction establishment, the large and magnificent El Placer building, El Dorado, Hotel de Mejico, Drs. WE FREDERICK the SEVENTH by the Grace of God King ot Donmark, of the Vandals and Goths, Duke of Schleswig, Holstein, Stormarn, Ditmarch, Lauenburg &. Oldenburg, M are known : Having most graciously commanded Our beloved Fedderse.v, Governor of Our Possessions in the West Indies, to proceed without delay to the Islands, in order to assume his office, with the powers now pertaining to the same, We have, at the same time, most graciously commissioned him to cause some well-informed and respectable persons to he appointed as a committee at Christiansted, presided over by himself, to consider and report to Us upon a draft of a colonial law for Our W est India Possessions, which draft he will lay before them. We entertain the hope, that the Inhabitants of Our West India Possessions will receive this as a new proof of Our Royal Favor and of Our solicitude lor the true welfare of the population, and We feel confident, that Ye by loyalty, industry and every civic virtue will prove qualified for that extension of civil rights, which We intend to secure to You by a colonial law. Given at Our Palace of Frederichsborg, the 16th of May in the year of our Lord One Thousand Eight Hundred and Fifty One. Under Our IIoyai, Hand and Seal. FREDERIK R. L. 8. K.

LIFE IN THE NORTH. by FRED ERIK A BREMER. Continued from our last. From the problem of the inner life, we will now pass to that of the outer ; to that which the great struggle of the day is endeavoring to solve. There appears to some to be a gulf between these, but we do not regard it as such, and we will cast some light upon it. In political development the Scandinavian North does not stand behind, but rather takes the lead of the lively people of the South. The freedom of the people is an old idea up in the North. Its sovereignty was first acknowledged in Sweden, later in Norway, latest in Denmark þÿ but there it is most supreme. The political evolution which, without revolution, has lately occurred in Denmark þÿ and which has changed the government from an absolute to a constitutional monarchy", based 011 democratic principles, has nevertheless roots which Powerful must the nation become, as strike back into remote times. And it may be said that the absolute monarch, Frederick the Third, commenced the enfranchisement of the people which, continued by Frederick the Sixth, was ompleted by Frederick the Seventh. þÿ This wa6 accomplished unanimously by king and people in a moment of great outward danger, when the country was attacked by a powerful enemy. Then did king and people join together and stand as one man, ready to offer up goods and life for the common fatherland, for the right and honor of Denmark. This grand movement, which still swells in the heart of the people, has given a strong impulse to the high-

est moral and political development, and a new strength to monarchy in the North. Neither lias the spirit of freedom called forth here any of those darker phenomena which have gloomed and thrown back the development of freedom in other countries. The strife between gods and giants still goes forward in this day. Which shall become the conqueror ? We look back with hope to the oldest history of the North, to that prophecy which is contained in the appearance of he first settlers in the North, under the peaceful guidance of Asarna, and to the people's voluntary homage to their superior wisdom. We look upon the great rising middlelass, which daily grows in the North, bv J additions from the aristocratic order, as well as from the artisan-classes, who inake labor their honor, and the noblest humanity the object of their education- We behold an emancipation, in the best sense of the word, which elevates more and more the subjected classes, and levels the separating barriers of rank a. ul fashion. Lastly we look with confidence upon of mentioned and the oldest sanctuary of the North, on domestic life and on home. We see the home as it was there formcrlv, " a holy room." utiassailed by the storms either

8W ATIS, of times or seasons, as it was of old, and more than of old, a home for the divine powers of truth, of fidelity, of self-sacrificing love. We see the , the life which prevailed this winter in sacrificial hearth stand in the home, and the altar in the church in the Northern Land, and upon this we build our trust that here the development of freedom will become mighty without its dark side ; that here the people will not misunderstand that natural, needful aristocracy, which is founded by the ordination of the Creator, which consists in a true superiority, above all, in that which the human being acquires for himself by ability and virtue. Does not the proþÿ phetic Iduna stand in the circle of the Northern gods, goddess at the same time of youth and piety, bearing with her the fruit of renovation, that without which the very gods must become old. The authority of the people is, in reality, the object for which the people are striving, and which they sooner or later will attain an object far higher, and far þÿ nobler than mere worldly prosperity. þÿ

well as the individual, who, by free-will alone, without any compulsory outward power, knows how to determine its own destiny. But powerful is no one, and great is no one in any degree, who does not acquire rule over (the word must be spoken for a truer can not be found) his own sinful heart. The kindred people of the North seem to be called upon by character and history, as well as by the development of the nations, to set an example to other people by a noble, peaceful, and independent life. The spring approaches. It seems as if this year would come early in the North. Nature comes forth to her festival of gladness. Shall human beings advance against each other in the work of destruction ? That is the question of the day. In Denmark they are arming for war, and upon the blue waters of the Mound, lloats the crimson flag of the war-ships, floats " Dannebrog. We acknowledge that all our sympathies are for this beautiful land, for the amiable people here, for a nation of faithful subjects, and of oppressed peasants, who from Schleswig called on the mother-country for aid, and, as in the peasant Lauriz Skau, found an interpreter possessed of the most fervid eloquence. We have already referred to the silent work of peace which is going forward here, and which is preparing a future lor Denmark, over which war and death can not have any real power. Peaceful and fruitful seasons, good rulers and statesmen have, during the last thirty years, made the land rich and happy.t

Little Denmark is for the present one of the most flourishing and best-governed states of Europe. t The sense of this National Flag. t Among the remarkable statesmen ought to he I'rofessou IlAvin, an industrious improver prisons prison discipline in this country. t The active educational spirit in the country, and the consequent great demand for men of knowledge and ability, have very much conduced to the formation of a distinguished class of our officials, who now contribute greatly to the strength of the nation
increases the naturally buoyant and sanguine temper ot the people. Nothing can be a stronger testimony of this than

Copenhagen, just at the conclusion of one war, and when another was threatening to break out. At 110 time had tingenius of the poets, and the author.-, been more prolific ; at 110 time bad the public been more receptive, more inclined to read, or more interested by poetry and romance ; and never, for many years, had the Exhibition of the Academy of Printers displayed such an affluence of remarkable works. Neitlur were purchasers of these wanting, although they continued to contribute liberally to the help of those who I d suffered by the war, and 10 other benevolent objects. " Denmark," say the Danes, " is a good little fellow ; be lias at Ho same time a good heart and a heavy purse." And thus stands he undaunted, ready for war as for peace. War! we will not believe it ! it seems almost irrational, that, at the present day, bloody war should arise between two highly civilized nations; it seems almost an injustice to them to believe that they can not settle a dispute without blows ; that they can not come to an amicable adjustment of their differences. It seems to those who are quietly looking on, as if people had now something better to do than to kill one another ; as it the time were come when the spirits of the þÿpeople like the heroes around King Arthur's table þÿ might con e together, as into a great castle-hall, io tell one another, their legends and fairyþÿtales and llolgcr, the Dane, knows wonderful ones þÿ! to entertain one another. and drink together in peace and

good fellowship, and to wrestle and strive together on their hills in the glorious combat of mind. And have they not already begun to do so ? Have not the people of the earth, within the last few years, visited one another by the paths ot mind, on the wing-- of steam, kindly entertained by each other's wealth, and enriched thereby? The Scandinavian people have done this among themselves in a still deeper sense than other nations. They have, in consequence of this new acquaintance, acknowledged each other as brethren. And the consciousness of that union, for which they were formed, both by nature and spirit, has now become loo slrong for any outward, accidental circumstance to destroy. It is a union of heart and intelligence, a spiritual bond, out of which ascends for the future a lofty and glorious life in the North. We intended here to have concluded, and we ought perhaps to have done so, but þÿ we could not. We find ourselves prevented by many little magical beings, which despotically seize upon our inclination and our heart, and compel us to pay attention to them, and they are right. To he eon t i mted.

H E FREDERICK the SEVENTH by the Grace of God King of Denmark, of the Vandals and Goths, Duke of Sclilcswig, Holstein, Siortnarn, Ditinarch, Lauenburg & Oldenburg, Make known : Having most graciously commanded Our beloved Feddersen, Governor of Our Possessions in the W est Indies, to proceed without delay to the Islands, in order to assume his office, with the powers now pertaining to the same, We have, at the same time, most graciously commissioned him to cause some well-informed and respectable persons to be appointed as a committee at Christiansted, presided over by himself, to consider and report to I s upon a draft of a colonial law for Our West India Possessions, which draft he will lay before them. We entertain the hope, that the Inhabitants of Our West India Possessions will receive this as a new proof of Our Royal Favor and of Our solicitude for the true welfare of the population, and We feel confident, that Ve by loyalty, industry and every civic virtue will prove qualified for that extension of civil rigiits, which We intend to secure to You by a colonial law. LIFE IN TIIE NORTH. BY FKEDERIKA UKEMElt. Concluded. We began by speaking of the neglected, the least happily circumstanced cliildren in Denmark ; we ought not to end without saying a few words about the fortunate little ones, the many who are guarded by the tenderness of parents, whom the sun of fortune shines upon, about the most beautiful buds on the tree | pride of Denmark's future. They are too lovable for us not to notice them nearer for , len, þÿ a moment. And that can easily be done if vou will walk into the neighborhood of the King's New Market, or into the royal gardens at the Castle of Rosenborg, wliere the little boy of stone rides m such wild merriment on the swan, and, as if in terror, or in very joyfulness, throws up six beautiful water-jets, which, clear as crystal, glitter in the sun. There you may see many ot the little ones with their "gold-nurses, peasant-women from Hedebo, with their broad-bordered green petticoats, broad ribbons, red or black, hanging front their necks a long way down their backs. And what backs! þÿ so broad and stately! One can really put confidence in these women from a glance at their backs ; and when one sees their countenances bearing the stamp of health and honesty, one is only the more confirmed in one's opinion. These women must have been made on purpose to have the care of children. But it was about the little ones 1 was going to speak, the dearly beloved Danish children. Describethem I can not, neither portray them, which is a pity. But more lovely children 1

never saw, neither in Sweden nor Norway, in England nor France, Switzerland nor Holland. Yes, I am certain of this þÿ that they would, if it c; me to the trial, captivate even Germany. June 1st. Spring is now in full bloom, and advances toward Midsummer. The islands of Denmark have put on their glorious attire. The beech-woods murmur by the blue creeks ; the groves are become vocal ; the stork lias arrived ; the meadows arc in bloom ; the golden locks ol the laburnum stream in the wind. But there arises no joyful song of human voices from the friendly islands. Tears, bitter tears, the tears of mothers, wives, brides, sisters, fall upon the beautiful Hower-clad earth. Ah! war has again broke out, and many sons of the country have fallen, and still fall in the hopeless combat against a conquering superior force. A little band of men stand lighting against a host composed of their own number many times multiplied þÿ one million against thirty millions. llow can there be, any hope V And yet, wonderful but true, there is no doubt, no despondency in that little band ; such firm faith have they in their own righteous cause, and in the righteous arbitrator of the people's fate. the temper and disposition the Danish Nothing can more truly of characterize people, than the effect which lias been produced by that unfortunate affair at Eckerntbrdc. The tidings of this reached Copenhagen on Easter-eve. What a murmur of sorrowful disquiet there was that evening in the city, especially in

the neighborhood of the post-house. Sorrow and amusement were upon every countenance. People talked to each other without the ceremony of introduction ; high and low communicated to each other what they had heard, what they knew, and what they thought, and wept together. It was as Easter had lost a child. On if every family Sunday,

the people streamed into the churches. The preachers spoke publicly troia the pulpits, of the great misfortune which had occurred, lamenting, comforting, and encouraging. The immortal theme of death, and the resurrection, had a new and an irresistible significant- þÿ The people listened and wept. It wis like a day of humiliation in Israel. T ie misfortune of the fatherland was the misfortune of every individual. The blow which had struck the maritime power of Denmark, struck the silent and hope of every heart. 1 saw young not girls for the shed tears, not for the fal- dead, but for " our Gefion for Dannebrog !" That was Easter Sunday. On Easter Monday all was silent in were hagen. The theatres the gay Copen- closed; the dejected attendants spoke whispers in ; nothing was to be heard but sighs a d conversation about the broken hearts ol wives and brides. That was the second d »y. On the third, life again raised itselfwiih strength. Volunteer sailors came by fundi eds, came singing to offer themselves in the place of those who, at Eckernfdrde, ii ui fallen either by death, or into the bands of the enemy. Contributions of money paration poured in from all for sides for war, the for a new pre- families of the killed and wounded. The rich gave abundantly of their wealth, the poor widow gave her note, and the mothers (beautiful to say) encouraged their sous to go and light tor the fatherland. A few days later, and the public mind was again calm and collected, and the theatres were aga n full of people.

But all hearts, all noble feelings, seemed to have opened their fountains for a more abundant flow. The Dui.sh. people were now of only one great who, in the day sorrow, <;r iv nearer family, together, to comfort and to support each other. We will here permit ourselves to introduce a little trait, which will show the feeling of these days. Among the many who were named in the newspapers as having fallen at Ekernfbrde, was a young man who had not fallen, and who, having saved himself in an almost miraculous manner, returned unexpectedly Copenhagen, and to his to home there. His mother and l:is sisters sate in their mourning, which they had ju-t prepared, when, all at once, the lost son and brother stood among them! The mother must have died ot joy at the moment, had not a strong, secret person sion filled her mind that her son lived, and thus she was prepared for the sur prise. The news of this circumstance went þÿ wild-fire through Copenhagen.- like People rushed from house to house, into the coffee-houses, and to the newsrooms to announce it. All were glad, all rejoiced as if they had recovered a beloved brother. Tears of joy and sympathy fell from all eyes. People began to hope that other fallen on s mig! t likewise arise to return. Strangers to the happy family hastened to tlieni (o express their joy and their sympathy, and to embrace him who had returned. The whole city was one family of love. Days, weeks, months have passed since this, and the war continues: coun-

þÿ tenances grow dark, and the foe goes on conquering. But calm and firm stands the little nation, determined to dare to the utmost, and to fight to the last drop of blood. There is now no song of rejoicing upon the beautiful islands, neither is there any lamentation. They prepare for new efforts, for new sacrifices Th»re is a strong will, r

great courage, and a great patience in the Danish people at this time. No one can see it without emotion, or without admiration. And therefore þÿ " Kindly islands, enchanting islands ! whether tears still longer fall upon your soil, whether the enemy shall suck your marrow, and the trial become still severer: friendly islands blessed are ye still !" There is an honor, a victory, an immortality, which every people, as well a 8 every man, can acquire for himself, even when apparently subjected to an outward superior power. And therefore þÿ tears of Denmark's daughters þÿfall fall still, it it must be so ! The soil which you water, is the soil of the hero, and that noble sorrow is the mother of a noble joy. You shall live to see that which has been sown in bitterness, bearing the sheaves of a noble harvest, and your beloved Dannebrog waving in joy over the waters of Denmark þÿ over the blue billows. When the life of a people is what it is here at this time; then awakes its genius; then it is at hand with a saving power. The genius of Denmark has said : When life blooms forth in tlie heart of the Dane, When their song the people raises, Then bright as the sun do I live again, And the poets sing my praise9. My name it known to the toiling hind, I embrace him with exultation, With joy my life renewed, I find I live in the heart of the nation. Thou know'st it, peasant ! I am not dead ; I come back to thee in my glory ! f am thy faithful helper in need. As in Denmark's ancient story

At this moment, shortly after I wrote down the foregoing lines, the glad tidings of Denmark's great victory over the Revolutionists of I'redericia, on the 5th of July, resounded through Copenhagen. If nation ever deserved triumph, it is Denmark at this time from the manner in which it has borne adversity, and now receives victory. At this moment joy is counterbalanced by sorrow for the many fallen. All l'ear for their beloved. The death of the brave General Rye is universally lamented. But it is well with him ! The 5th of July was his birthday. " I intend to celebrate this day in a remarkable manner," wrote he, shortly before, to his wife, " whether it brings me victory, or whether it leaves me in the field of battle." It was on the 5th of July when be won a victory, and died the death of a hero, at the moment when, after having had two horses shot under him, lie, on foot, again led the assault against the enemy's " Nay, my battery, children ! there is no talking calling to his people, to-day of a retreat!" We therefore most graciously command You, on Your arrival in the Islands, to direct the several Burgher Councils to elect as soon as possible, each in behalf of its own Island, men qualified for the above purpose, four for St. Croix, three for St. Thomas and one for St. Johns, whereupon You .will select two men, whom V oil, on mature consideration, may deem well adapted to complete, in behalf of all the Islands, the election of the Burgher Councils for the purpose aforesaid. These ten men will then have to meet at Christiansted, on a day appointed by You, and after having been made uc-

We are tempted to offer a few remarks on His Majesty's late Letter Patent, which has caused such joy and exultation in the minds of all classes of people here, more particularly from the tender manner in which Our beloved Sovereign addresses us, and the kind promises held out to us for an extension of our civil rights. His Majesty has, in this document, been most graciously pleased to declare, that Governor FEDDERSEN is commissioned to cause some well-informed and respectable persons to be appointed as a committee at Cliristiansted, presided over by His Excellency, to consider and report to His Majesty upon a draft of a Colonial Law for his West India possessions. The committee to be appointed at Christiansted will, (as far as regards St. Croix,) be composed of the Burgher Council, who will appoint some additional members. This being done, and other preliminaries entered into, the draft of the colonial law will then belaid before them, to considerand report with regard to its contents. þÿ It may not, however, be superfluous to state, that the Burgher Council as the Representative of the people will consider seriously on the many advantages to be derived f rom a well-regulated and wisely-framed Colonial-Law ; as the draft, doubtless, is intended to embody an extension of the political and religious rights of the inhabitants of the dauish westindia islands. Should there, unfortunately, be any wiseacres or men of narrow-minded views among this body of our Representatives; let them, we say, re-

main quiet and refrain from exposing themselves, or injuring our cause and let the extra members be men of good sense and sound experience, and above all, men totally devoid of prejudice. If these hints arc taken, we have nothing to tear ; but, on the contrary, may expect a golden harvest as the result ot the meeting.

oOo- From the St. Thomas '1 imes, June 28. Our columns of to-day are occupied with important official announcements, w Inch will prove highly acceptable to out leaders. Every word contained in His Most Gracious Majesty's Letter Patent, breathes the spirit of a purely constitutional and citizen Monarch. Let the inhabitants of these Islands then see to it, that the golden privileges offered them, be not permitted to escape without benefit. We feel particularly anxious to discover by what mode the Members of the Committee for drafting a I Colonial Law" are to be selected. Of course there will be a goodly sprinkling of aspirants, among whom will figure no inconsiderable number ol those who arc characterized as members of the Anc.ien " Regime who would convey to the commission their old cherished paternal
views, viz., everything for the people, nothing by the people. We repeat, let then the communities of these Islands watch over with anxious care the publi, right which has thus been extended to them.

We have to report the arrival here yesterday afternoon of of the American Brig Commayuid, Boston, Captain Dam ei. Brown. The Cummaquid was bound to New Orleans, from Thomastown, Maine, with a cargo of temper lime; and alter being eleven days at sea, it was discovered that she was on lire, occasioned by the combustion of the lime in her hold. The wind being south-westerly, she was unable to makeany port in the United States, and con scquently her hatches were battened down, and she made for this Port. She was spoken at sea by three other vessels, when every assistance was tender ed. hot Captain Brown thought it pru dent not to quit the vessel, and had his boats in readiness in case of need. A survey has been held lo-day on the ve?m !, but we have not heard the decision of the Board. We, however, opine that she will ultimately lie condemned, as tiie lime continues to burn up to lo-dav þÿ ibid.

" Horse-shoe" Reef, and was immedi ately boarded by the ever watchful Anc gadians, who soon stripped Iter from " truck to keelson." It is, however, ap parent that since the late frequent visits of the British Sloop-of-War Helena, to that place, the inhabitants have par for,' become a little more honest, þÿ as tinarticles saved on this occasion, viz the þÿ molasses, sails, spars, rigging. ST. CROIX AVIS. Cliibtianstrd, 9th June I 831. We beg to lay before our readers, the Address, which was presented to His Excellency Governor Hansen, on Monday last the 2nd instant, and the Reply of His Excellency:

Address: We the undersigned Planters, Merchants, and others, deeply interested in the welfare of this Island, take leave, respectfully to address your Excellency, on the occasion of your intended removal from this Government, a circumstance which we all most sincerely lament, we had hoped that your Excellency, would much longer have remained among us, and witnessed the progressive improvement emanating from your þÿExcellency s verv judicious Regulations. On your þÿExcellency s arrival, you found the Colony in a very disorganised state, and every thing in a most unsatisfactory condition, occasioned by the great change which had then but recently taken place, in our social relations. þÿ Gentlemen, Tour Excellency immediately saw the necessity for it, and caused to be framed, ind promulgated ; that wise, equitable md most beneficial code of regulations tor the guidance of the agricultural portion of the community, which at once inspired confidence, and arrested in some measure, the declining value of property, which without them, would have become valueless ; We have had the experience of their good effects, for upwards of two years and a half, and we can assure your Excellency that our early convictions of their soundness and utility have been satisfacfSrily confirmed in the good order, and conduct, of the working class. It must be as gratifying to your Excellency, as it is to ourselves to know this, and that these regulations, have been appreciated, and applauded

in many of the British Islands, and rceivcd strong encomiums from a high public functionary in one of the most important of the Colonies; and, also, from a well known writer on West Indian Agriculture (in which he is well ersed) who in speaking of Sit. Croix and its regulations, thus expresses himself. . : Hie wisdom and efficiency of those well known ordinances for the regulalion of labour, which framed and digested with a singular amount of lirmþÿ ness, benevolence, and justice, have worked admirably in so tiding you þÿ þÿ through a period of great difficulty, as, to have secured for your Island, not " only a þÿ degree prosperity, of which one hardly dared, sometime ago to anticiþÿ but an pate, honourable þÿdistinction. In the measure to which we allude, as well as in every other, connected with the Island, and proposed by your Excellency, we unhesitatingly express our linn conviction, that your Excellency has been actuated by a sincere desire to uphold the honor and interest of the Government, and to promote, the peace, order, and welfare of the Island !

With our sincere good wishes for your health, happiness, and prosperity, W e remain

I should fail in due recognition of your kindness did 1 not endeavour to thank you for the indulgent judgement you have passed on me, in the address I have had the honor to receive on the occasion of my approaching departure from this colonv. You have been pleased to allude iu terms of approbation to certain laws i and regulations passed by me during the time the government of this island has been entrusted to me. I feel content, and 1 am well rewarded should my endeavours have been beneficial to the community at large, and I can speak on this point without affected modesty and without apparent acception of all what you have said in my favor, because 1 claim no other merit but having had temper to listen to, and judgement to adopt the excellent advice which has been tendered to me by enlightened, experienced and practical men, who have stood by me through bad report, and through good report. H e have fallen upon hard times, and have succeeded partially to conquer the most pressing dillicultics. In mentioning this 1 shall not omit to bear witness to the loyalty and to the patience with which all classes of this community, the poor as well as the more fortunate of the inhabitants, have supported their troubles. The reward will not be withheld. Happier days are dawning upon you, and, by the blessing of God, abundant riches are adorning your fields. 1 deeply regret being obliged to leave you at a time when it will be possible, I trust, to carry through measures for the improvement of local affairs, which

have been partially prepared but hitherto delayed by circumstances, over which 1 had no control. If 1 dare indulge myself in listening to your friendly assurances, þÿ 1 leave you however with the consolation of having secured the good will ol a considerable number of my fellow

citizens. In return for your kindness I beg to assure you, that absent as well as present I shall consider myself always liable to be called upon to support your interests, and always leady to obey the summons. I have the honor to be, Gentlemen, your sincere friend and faithful servant. (Signed) 1. HANSEN. Government House, St. Croix, June 2nd 1851.

While the more populous cities of Europe and America are crowded to their utmost capacity', and to repletion, with the pool and destitute of both sexes, seeking but not able to find, employment, whereby life may be prolonged vet a feu days or years, no matter bow much mise ry and degradation may be endured in the struggle; where men, women and children, by thousands and ten hundreds of thousands, give themselves up to crime, debauchery, despair and death, for the want of the opportunity of earning an honest livelihood, here, on this whole Pacific coast, exists the finest, openings for the exercise of any kind of labour. More especially is this true as relates to the Isthmus and city of Panama. To prove tln, let us give a few facts and figures. For instance, there is u great demand here now, and will be for years to come, þÿ for carpenters. W c are told that the most indifferent workmen obtain four, five, or six dollars a day. Painters are wanted at from eight to ten dollars a day. There is not an American or English Blacksmith shop in town. An enterprising, steady, industrious master carpenter, who would come herewith ten or twenty journeymen, we do verily believe, would require but two or three years, to become independent. The worthy persons at present engaged in the business here, frequently have shop work engaged one or two mouths ahead. The constant pulling down of old, arid putting up of new houses þÿ 1 he repairing and refitting the numerous old

and dilapidated ones, to make room for the daily increasing American and other foreign population, would furnish immediate and constant employment to a vast number of these workmen. We believe there is not a professional bricklayer in the þÿplace and hut very few bricks ! þÿ Houses not built of wood, are constructed principally of a rough soft stone, peculiar to the country. Why will not some enterprising mason come here, and bring with him one of the numerous brick machines so common in our own country? The finest material in the world exists here, for the manufacture of brick, and a market l ight here in Pa nama, will be found for all 1 hat ciw be manufactured for years to come. Panama is rising, with a rapidity that is almost incredible. She 1ms slept for ages, and. had almost died out of the remembrance 1 of the world, but the acquisition of Cali

for nia by the United States, and the consequent immense immigration this way, has instilled into her new life and new prospects, and there is no telling when she will cease growing. To meet the wants ot those who settle or pass through here, great changes have to he made. The old hare walls and choked up streets, are giving way to rough and temporary improvements, which would he of a more extensive and permanent nature, if workmen could be had at any price, to make them so. The great secret of all this go-a-head-a-tiveness ; proceeds not from a momentary or fluctuating cause. It is the natural forerunning consequence of the incoming of the Great Atlantic and Pacific Pail Road! W e residents here know that this great work is making rapid strides towards completion, and that every pile driver, in its track is the foundation for a new house to be built here in Panama. While it conies on to meet us, we go out to meet þÿit In the course of two years it will be completed þÿ by that time, the many beautiful, and at present unoccupied and waste sites, less than a mile from the city walls, will he laid oil into regular streets, and beautiful and commodious dwellings and stores will then have tiie place now occupied by the stately cocoa nut tree, or the thick and apparently impenetrable undergrowth. þÿ Scarcely a steamer arrives at Chagres, that does not bring among its passengers, one or more families, to reside at Panama. Six months since, we knew of but three or four American ladies in

th<> place þÿ now there are more than a dozen þÿ and nearly all are keeping house. This creates a demand for imported house-hold þÿservants the natives of this i country being worse than useless to an \merican family. The average price ! tor an Irish female liouse-servant is from twenty to twenty-five dollars per month ; the wages of such cooks, as we have here, is rarely less than thirty-five dollars, and from that to þÿfifty the average is about forty. And such cooks ! Many of them perhaps, never lmilt a fire tor cooking purposes, before they came here! And yet þÿ help is so scarce, that any one can readily obtain employment at some of the above figures. Two or Mirec dozen good washer-women and miners, can find constant work, at from one to six dimes per piece. Taking a shirt, as a criterion, the usual cost of having it washed and ironed here, is lrom twenty to twenty-five cents þÿ and then if it is returned home, any time within fifteen or twenty days, the owner of it considers himself fortunate. We might go on with the enumeration of such facts as these, ad infinitum, hut we have said enough, no doubt, to convince all those under whose eye this article may fall, that in nny and every capacity þÿ except at clerking, labor is always in demand here, and at prices hotter than those now, upon an average, realized in California. (From the Demerara Royal Gazette. May 27.) By the CuriiQuanuur we have received Surinam papers to the 23rd instant. They contain some important Government regulations for carrying into effect the Royal Order of the Oth February lal respecting the slaves. These regulations, which form an entire new Slave Code, are too lengthy for us to go through the whole of them at present. We may safely say, however, that they appear to be one great step more made by the Government of the Netherlands towards final emancipation, and, however they may be received by the planters, that they evince much solicitude for the improvement ot' the lot of the slaves. In defining the amount of labour to he rendered by the slaves on plantations, the principle adhered to in these regulations is not to state the number of hours daily during which the slave shall be found to work, hut the emount of work which he shall give his master daily. In this respect the Dutch Government seem to have taken a leaf out ot our hook. The principle, therefore, upon which slavery in Surinam may now he considered to rest is that of compulsory task-work.

And such is the life of the North at this moment. I speak of the Scandinavian North ; and, as an auspicious star conducts me at this time to that part of it where this life is in the most lively activity, that is to Denmark, 1 will converse with you a little upon it, as it there appears. Zealand with rich ^cornfields, old town, with old, proud memories, cairns, and castles, ; Funcn, with its orchards, its fine estates, its wealthy farms? Around the large islands, dusters a wreath of small, often very small ones, which also abound with great recollections, some from the time of the Sagas, some from later ages, and which have fostered many a great man for the common mother-country. ThereJjreathes fresh, kindly, vernal life over these islands, amid which, swell the waves of the Atlantic, with the Cattegat, the Baltic, and North Sea. This harmonizes with the spirit of the people; for, not-

withstanding- the solemn memories of the ancient times, notwithstanding the stamp of the northern spirit in the char acter of family and popular life, it can not he denied that Scandinavia has in Denmark its link with southern Europe; and that the southern life shows itself among these Danish people, combined with Ihc natural liveliness of disposition and manners of the islanders. The Danes have, of late years, undergone a great change, yet, without losing their peculiar character. They have been born to a new life, or rather they have awoke to a consciousness of their own proper life. There comes frequently a spring n the life of a people, when the inner life, as it were, bursts its hands and blossoms forth vigorously. These are the times when a people creates energetically for itself a living unity am a people, an eternal, undying genius with a peculiar existence, a peculiar mission in the history of mankind. And such a time does not come all at once, as by a stroke of magic. No ! silent streams from the fountains of life, silent, influences of Ihc sun, quickening winds, storms, or zephyrs, prepare it long beforehand. So in this case. All the pure patriotism, all the great capacity of the humanly great ; that which genius and virtue have effected through the men and women of Denmark ; which the great kings of this

little country, its warriors and poets have accomplished, through the past centuries for the þÿnation honor, s lor the good of the people, lor the advancement of this spring, of which we speak, all this we must leave unmentioned ; little indeed of it has the historian recorded in any case. Who on earth knows the source of the Nile? llut we .advert to these things that we may not he wanting in justice and respect. The spring is come ; the spring which they nohlv prepared, and I will now speak ol its tellectual phenomena as they have developed themselves within the present century, and especially within the last twenty or thirty years ; as I have seen them, and jee them at this moment, in actual life. Regard this fugitive sketch as a faint attempt to reflect the impressions and þÿ he pictures forever stamped on the heart's memory. On Christmas live, 1848 þÿ a chill and cloudy þÿwinter evening s þÿ I found myself :n Copenhagen, in a large hall, where more than a hundred children, boys and girls, sung, danced, and made a joyous clamor around a lofty Christmas-tree, glittering with lights, flowers, fruits, cakes, and sweetmeats, up to the very ceiling. But brighter than the lights in the tree, shone the gladness in the eyes ol the children, and the bloom of health on their fresh countenances. A handsome, portly, middle-aged lady, in black, went round atmhg the children, with a motherly grace, examining their work in j luntlirnpic sewing and handicraft arts, encouraging and and rewarding them in an affectionate

manner. The children pressed around her, and looked up to her, all seeming to love, none to fear her. It was a charity-school in which I found myself : it was þÿDenmark mother- s ly, hut childless queen, Carolina Amalia, rhom I saw thus surrounded by poor children, whom she had made her own. It was a beautiful scene ; and what 1 ,,uv here was also an image of a life, a movement which, at this time, extends þÿ hrough the whole social life of the north It is the motherly, the womanly movement in society, expanding itself to the comprehension of a wider circle, to the care of the whole race of children, beyond the limits of home to the enfranchisement, the elevation of all neglected infancy. It is the maternal advance from the individual life into the general, to the erection of a new home. The asylum is its expanded embrace. þÿ Here wc have Nile-sources in society, There Christian love makes restitution for the injustice of fortune ; there the child seems to escape from the faults and calamities of its parents, to be preserved lor society at large, and to be educated for its benefit. Silently proceeds the maternal power to give a new birth to the human race, in its earliest years. And we rely on this power more than on any other on earth, for the accomplishment of this work, if ever such a new birth is really to take place ; and that the women of the North more dearly seem to accept this mission, and that the queens of the North, Carolina Amalia,

<8 21 of Denmark, and Josephina, of Sweden, march at the head of this maternal movement, it is only a duty to acknowledge. Nor do these ladies confine themselves to the care of childhood alone ; they extend their beneficial activity through a variety of channels to the children of misfortune, to the solitary, the sick, the old and neglected in society, who are sought out and assisted or con soled by the more fortunate. Blessed is material help in the hearts of t he needy ; hut still more blessed is the inresult which is effected by the personal affectionate sympathy of the rich, whether in intellectual or worldly wealth, for the poor in society. To this activity, an activity not less on the part of the men, associates itself, supporting it, and continuing it where it ceases. We will merely give one example of this. About thirty years ago, there swarmed in the streets of Copenhagen, a multitude of lads, from ten to fifteen years of age, like that still greater number in Stockholm, who are called þÿ harborþÿscamps, repulsive race, filthy gar- a in ments, and with wild, thievish eyes, the children of crime and misery, and growing up all wickedness, forever on the in watch for robbery and mischief. A government officer, who about that time received an appointment in the police, Mr:. A. Dkewson, was struck by the prevalence of this class, laid it to heart, and. with other similiarly disposed and phi men, formed a plan to extir pate this growing evil by a thorough searching remedy. When he had

matured his scheme, he called on his fellow-citizens for assistance. He did not call in vain. Liberal subscriptions flowed in from all sides, and, by their means, the young criminals were speedily removed from the capital to the remote provinces, where they were placed in good and orderly families, chiefly those of farmers. Transplanted into a rich soil, these young shoots of vice, almost wholly changed their nature, and became good and serviceable members of society, while ever since this period, the amount of crime in the capital has signally decreased, and the public good has as sensibly increased under the continued culture of the hitherto neglected youth. Very rarely now is the eye or the mind shocked in the streets of Copenhagen by the sight of mendicant children.

It has been asserted, as frequently as the annual budget has been brought forward for consideration, that the Colonies are ruinously expensive to the Parent as State, and are not worth retaining, yet soon as an attempt is made to relieve the Parent Government, to a considerable extent, of this expense, and to establish a policy bv which the Colonies taught ""self-reliance," the measure might be is denounced as being unwise ; and it is argued that the withdrawal of the iresent military establishments would lie " to abandon the whole of our Colonial possessions, and being once abandoned, other Countries would be invited to come forward and bid for them. But Lord John Russel explains why the retention ot the rays, the question was a most import- Colonics is expedient. His Lordship " ant one, for it was not a question ol saving money, but of the maintenance or desolation of the empire." Here we have it

it length acknowledged that the Colonies ire not so worthless after all; and so lar is the West Indies are concerned, it is our opinion that on an honest calculation, the declaration of their being enorexaggerated. entirely fallacious, is yet mously expensive will to be be found il not It our belief materially that the revenue derived from an excessive duty on sugar and other West Indian produce is or ought to be sutlicicnt to maintain the military establishments in these Colonies, and if we are correct here, it follows that it is not the Imperial Government, but the Colonies, that are maintaining the troops ; and with ordinary reduction the fact might have been perceived, and placed to the credit of the Colonies. For instance, last year the exportation to Great Britain, of sugar ilone, from this Island, amounted to bT.COO cwts., which, at 10s. Government luty, yielded the sum ol £48,800! an amount, in all conscience quite enough o maintain the handful of troops slaioncd in Grenada. The inhabitants of the West Indies dread no internal violence. If the bulk if the population were quiet and wellbehaved when in a state of slavery, it is not reasonable to suppose that they will be turbulent while industriously laboring and enjoying the privileges and advantages of freedom. Hence we require no troops to maintain internal quiet; a wellorganized police will answer our purpose. And we ask not too much when we require that should the Imperial Government deem it necessary to keep up a

large armed force in the Colonies to maintain its own status among nations, t shoud pay the cost itself. Sir William Molesworth views not the question in this light, " and nixed it up with local self-govern- has improperly ment." West Indians do not seek to lie alienated from Great Britain when they ask for "local self-government," nor do they desire the withdrawal of to the mean What we understand them troops. is, hat they should have an Elective Council and an Elective Assembly (we speak of the Crown Colonies, as far the Elect- I

If. <8 'it D J X _ A 7 5 ive Assembly goes) so that enactments deemed necessary to meet the requirements of each particular Colony, may not be thwarted, or suffer unnecessary impediment, by being referred to a party irresponsible to The People. They require a local Executive, vested with power to sanction such enactments, and which would save the tedious routine of being obliged to transmit such enactments to the Executive of another Island for confirmation. They require that all cepting appointments to local oflices þÿ that of the Executive be filled þÿ not exfrom among the residents, natives or otherwise, of the Colonies, and that in every respect the Civil government of the Colonies should be left to the Colonists themselves. Surely these are not unreasonable demands. It is perfectly imaginary, to suppose that the granting of "self-government," as we understand and have above explained it, would lead to the results apprehended by the opponents of the measure in the llouse of Commons. West India Colonists are not loyal from coercion, but from patriotism ; and while they are desirous to have as much control over the management ol their own affairs, as is consistent with their ability to direct those affairs, they repudiate the idea of having any other than the government of their beloved Queen to be their national guardian and protector; and even if they had the offer of alienation, we pledge ourselves that not one man out of a hundred would evince the least dis-

position to change his allegiance. Under any circumstance these Colonies will remain co-operative stations to refider good service to Great Britain in time of emergency, and Lord John Russell betrays his ignorance of West India fidelity when he insinuates or asserts the contrary.

Ingeman is, in a stillbroader sense, perhaps, than Oehlenschliiger, popular a poet, and in him every thing which belongs to the character and the popular temper of Denmark, loving, deep-thoughted, quiet and vigorous at once, seems to have found life and expression. Ingeinan has created the historical romance of the North. This romance with its peculiar figures; its great dramatic scenes; its pure spirit; its deep feeling; its fresh life has given birth to two miracles. It has made the history of Denmark dear to the Swedes, and it has taught the peasantry of Denmark to read romances. þÿIngeman s romances have been read by the people of Denmark, as no other books have been, except the Bible and the Hymn-book. þÿ The peasant possesses them, and through them he takes an interest in the history of his country and in its monuments. þÿ On these subjects he can enlighten foreigners. In doing this he refers to the books of Ingeman, to obtain which he has gladly paid the money won by the sweat of his brow. In reading them he often forgets the time for sleep after the labor of the day. lie sits up late with his family that he may read Ingeinan. He can not do better. A great deal is said in our time about literature for the people. Much zeal is shown and much labor is spent, and books for the people arc prepared consisting of instructive treatises ; useful and learned compositions which arc sent forth to enlighten and educate the people. And the people read them

little or not at all. The people are poeical ; the people are romantic; the people are full of humor. They love old jtorics ; heroic poems, love-songs, ballads and jests. The people have a deeply religious feeling. The heart of life hrobs in their heart. Literature for þÿ hemmust be kindred to this heart ; must awake responses in all its strings. An author who can do this, while he elevates the moral sense and purities the taste, will be a favorite with the people, and will be their benefactor. þÿ lie will ennoble at the same time that he amuses. Ingeman does this. Ingeman is a man of truth. The germ of a high and holy understanding of life, and of every thing lies in all that he

In Denmark, much lias been done successfully in his way, ami þÿ the Society for the right use of the Freedom ot the þÿPress has understood its own business and the taste of the people. Above five hundred circulating libraries, calculated for the peasantry and he working-classes are at this time spread over Denmark ; and all that, is needed is to provide books nough to satisfy the desire for them. For forty years his th s society been in operation, thirty of which, under the direction of that zealous statesman, Privy- Counsellor Collin, and the results of Ins active exertions arc seen in the increasing taste of the peasantry and the handicraftmcn for pleasures of a higher order. Ale-houses and clubs arc less frequented ; the homo more beloved, and the readings in the lamily circle, during the autumn and winter evenings, givo a new delight and a new interest to family life.

Mr. Editor, Dear Sir ! Of late I have perused several communications regarding the Militia, in the columns of your paper. I must certainly agree in opinion with the writer of the communication to the Editor of the " St. Thomas Times," in so far as he objects "to play the soldier." A Militia is certainly useful ; hut where is the utility of monthly meetings? I know many men of childish minds, who decidedly take a pleasure in being put in a position, where tlicy can scoff at and scold their fellow-citizens with im

18.11, punity ; and who, like your correspondent " C" delight to play the soldier on the " Champ de Mars" þÿ (a very grand name for the pasturage beyond the town.) These monthly meetings are of comparatively little use, except in so far as they gratify the largely developed selfesteem of these sui disant Field Marshals. Resides, the idea is certainly ridiculous to see some 50 or <10 men marching, in as straight a line as the letter S þÿ up and down a parade ground (I should perhaps use the more fashionable term "Champ de Mars") until their commander gets either tired or hoarse, or I ioth, and dismisses them. Hut the evil does not stop here. The Land treasury has a yearly expense for t lie purchase of cartridges, 590 of which can be used by a company of 50 men on a drill day, for tlie only purpose of teaching the men to tire at one or the same lime, or as it is commonly expressed "like one man." 8urely the times are too enlightened for all tliis nonsence. If we must have a Militia, let us have one; but at the same time do not make it a useless and annoying burthen to the community. I assure you, Mr. Editor, you cannot conceive how the sight of one of these corps under drill gratifies my love of the ridiculous. Such awkward evolutions! And the Danish words of command þÿ Mil powers! It is murdered outright. To hear of the petty jealousies existing among these men of " rank" in the Militia corps, is also the source of amusement; especially when to substantiate their claims for promotion, they

tell of dangers braved with heart and soul in July 1848. Magnifying glasses appear to have been in universal use in those days, for 1 really cannot, nor did not, see liovv dangers could be anticipated from a class of persons who were scared and ran at the mere sound of " Ilvcm der," halloed out, I must confess, in no very melodious or pleasing manner. Still, very few of these men do not fancy that they have been in battle, forgetting at the same time, that they were minus an opponent. In conclusion, I must remark that 1 think it unfair that but a portion of the inhabitants of the town does Militia duty, while the greater number can for their amusemunt look on their fellowcitizens while under the torture of the Militia exercise I am, Sir, Yours, II

The knowledge of an extensively organized conspiracy embittered the last years of the Emperor Alexander, and increased his constitutional melancholy, llis attachment to Tzarsko Zeio made him linger longer at his summer palace than was prudent in a man subject to erysipelas. The wound in his leg reopened with very unfavorable symptoms, and he was compelled to leave his lavurite residence in a closed litter for St. Petersburgh ; and the skill and firmness ot Mr. W y Hie, his Scotch surgeon, alone saved the diseased limb from amputation. As soon as he was cured, he returned again to Tzarsko Zelo, where the spring found hiin as usual alone, without a court or chamberlain, only giving audience to his ministers twice a week. His existence resembled rather that of an anchorite weeping for the sins of his youth, than that of a great emperor who makes the happiness of his people. He regulated his time in the following manner: in summer he rose at live, and in winter at six o'clock every morning, and as soon as the duties of the toilet were ended, entered his cabinet, m which the greatest order was observed. | He found there a cambric handker- i chief folded, and a packet of new pens, lie only used these pens in signing his name, and never made use of them again. As soon as he had concluded this business, he descended into the garden, | Alexander where, notwithstanding the report of a
ed alone, with no other guards than the sentinels always stationed before the

palace ol \lcxander. \t live he returned, to dine alone, and after his solitary meal was lulled to sleep bv the melancholy airs played hy the military hand ot the guard regiment <>n dutv. The selection of the music was always made hy himself, and lie seemed to sink to repose, and to awake, with t lie same sombre dispositions and feelings which had been lus companions throughout the day. His empress. Elizabeth, lived like hei consort, in profound solitude, watching over him like an invisible angel. Time had not extinguished in her heart the profound passion with which the youthful Czarow itz had inspired her at first sight, ami which she had preserved in her heart, pure and inviolate, llis numerous and public infidelities could not stille this boh and beautiful attachment, which formed at once tiie happiness and ntiserv of ;i delicate and sensitive woman. At this period of her life, the empress at live-ami forty retained her fine shape ami noble carriage, w bile her countenance showed the remains of considerable beauty, more impaired by sorrow than time. Calumny itself bad never dared to aim ho r envenomed shafts at one so eminently chaste and good. Her presence demanded the respect due to virtue, still more than the homage proper lo her elevated rank. She resembled indeed more an angel exiled from heaven, than the imperial consort of a prince \v ho ruled a large portion of the earth. In the summer of 1825, the last he was destined to see, the physicians of the

emperor unanimously recommended a journey to the Crimea, as the best medicine he could take. Alexander appeared perfectly indifferent to a measure which regarded his individual benefit, but the empress, deeply interested in anv event likely to restore lier husband's health, asked and obtained permission lo accompany him. The necessaiy preparations for this long absence overwhelmed the emperor with business, and for a fortnight he rose earlier, and went to bed later, than was customary lo him. In the month of June, no visible alteration was observed in his appearance, and lie quitted St. l'eteisburgh after a service had been chanted, to bring (low u a blessing from above on his journey. þÿ He was accompanied by the empress, his faithful coachman Ivan, and some officers belonging to the staff' of Gene ral Diebitch. He stopped at Warsaw a few days, in order to celebrate the birthday of his brother, the Grand-Duke Constantine, and arrived at Tangaroff'in the end of August, 125. Both the illustrious travelers found their health benefited by the change of scene and climate. took a great liking to Tangarofl", a small town on the borders of the conspiracy which had existed two years i Sea of Azof, comprising a thousand illagainst his life and government, he walk- ! built houses, of which a sixth-part alone are of brick and stone, while the remainder resemble wooden cages covered with dirt. The streets arc large, but with omissions and addition hy Miss Jane Strickland ! then they have no pavement, and arc

alternately loaded with dust, or inundated with mud. The dust rises in clouds, which conceals alike man and beast under a thick vail, and penetrates every where the carefully closed jalousies with which the houses are guarded, and cov- j crs the garments of their inhabitants. þÿ The food, the water, are loaded with it; and the last can not be drunk till previ- j ouslv boiled with salt of tartar, which precipitates it; a precaution absolutely ches of Count WoronzofF. lie then dicnecessary to free it from this disagreeable and dangerous deposit. The emperor took possession of the governor's house, where he sometimes slept and took his meals. His abode there in the day-lime rarely exceeded two hours. The rest of his time was passed in wandering about the country on foot, in the hot dust, or wet mud. No weather put any stop to his out-door exercise, and no advice from Ins medical attendant nor warning from the natives ol'TangarotV, could prevail upon him to lake the slightest precaution against the fatal autumnal fever of the country. þÿ His principal occupation was planning and planting a great public garden, in which undertaking he was assisted hy an Englishman whom he had brought with him from St. Petersburg!) for that purpose. He frecpiently slept on the -pot on a camp-bed, with his head resting upon a leather pillow. If general report may he credited, planting gardens was not the principal object that engrossed the Hussion emperor's attention, lie was said to he employed in framing a new constitution

fir Uusmo, and unable to contend at St. Petersburg!) with the prejudices ol the aristocracy, had retired to this small iil\, for the purpose ol conferring this benefit upon his enslaved country. However this might he, the emperor did not slay long at a time at Tangaroll, where his empress, unable to share with h i in the fatigues of his long journeys, permanent l\ resided, during his frequent absences from his head-quarters. Alexander, in fact, hi ule rapid excursions to the country about the Ibin, and was sometimes at Tcherkask, sometimes at llonetx. He was on the eve of departure for Astraean, wlien tlount Woronzoff in person, came to announce to his sovereign, the existence of the mysterious conspiracy which had haunted liini in St. Petersburg!!, and which extended to the Crimea, where his personal presence could alone appease the general discontent. The prospect of traversing three hundred leagues appeared a trille to Alexander, whom rapid journeys alone diverted from his oppressive melancholy. He announced to the empress li is departure, which he only delayed till the return of messenger, he had sent to Alapka. The expected courier brought new details of the conspiracy, which aimed at the life, as well as the government of Alexander. This discovery agitated hitn terribly. lie rested his aching head on his hands, gave a deep groan, and exclaimed, " Oh, my father, my father !" Though it was then mid-

ass. A'trats. night, he caused Count Diehitch to lie | prive the suffering prince of the water, roused from sleep and summoned into his presence. The general, who lodged in the next house, found his master in a dreadfully excited state, now traversing the apartment with hasty strides, now throwing himself upon the lied with deep sighs and convulsive starts. He at length became calm, and discussed the intelligence conveyed in the dispat-

tated two, one addressed to the \ iceroy of Poland, the other to the Crand-Duke Nicholas. With these documents, all traces of his terrible agitation disappeared. He was quite calm, and his countenance betrayed nothing of the emotion that had harassed hint the preceding night. Count Worouzoff, notwithstanding this apparent calmness, found liini difficult to please, and unusually irritable, for Alexander was constitutionally sweettempered and patient, lie did not delay his journey on account of this internal disquiet, hut gave orders for ln> departure from Tangaroll', which he lixed for the following day. His ill-humor increased during the journey ; he complained of the badness of the roads and the slowness ol the horses, lie had never been known to grumble before. His irritation became more apparent when Sir James Wyllie, his confidential medical attendant, recommended him to take some precaution against the frozen winds of the autumn; for he threw away with a gesture of impatience the cloak and pelisse he uttered, anil braved the danger he had been entreated to avoid. Jlis imprudence soon produced consequences. þÿ That evening he caught cold, and coughed incessantly, and the following day on his arrival at OrielolV, an intermittent fever appeared, whic h soon alter, aggravated hv the obstinacy ol the invalid, turned to the remittent fevci common to TangarolVand its environs in the autumn. The emperor, whose increasing malady gave him a presage of his approach-

ing death, expressed a wish to return to the empress, arid once more took the route to Tonga rod'; contrary to the prayers of Sir James Wyllie, he chose to perform a part of the journey on horseback, but the failure of his strength dually forced him to re-enter his carriage. He entered Tangaroff on the fifth of November, and swooned the moment lie came into the governor's house. The empress, who was suffering with a complaint of the heart, forgot her malady, while watching over her dying husband. Change ot place only increased the fatal fever which prayed upon his frame, which seemed to gather strength from day to day. On the eighth, Wyllie called in Dr. Stephiegen, and 011 the thirteenth they endeavored to counteract the affection ol the brain, and wished to bleed the imperial patient, lie would not submit to the operation, and demanded iccd-water, which they refused. Their denial irritated him, and lie rejected every tiling they offered liini. These learned men were unwise to de-

a safe and harmless beverage in such fevers. In laet, nature herself sometimes. in inspiring the wish, provides the remedy. The emperor, 011 the afternoon of that day wrote and sealed a letter, when, perceiving the taper remained burning, he told Ins attendant to extinguish it, in words that plainly expressed his feelings in regard to the dangerous nature of his malady. " Put out that light, mv friend, or the people will take it for a bier candle, and will suppose 1 am already dead.'' On the fourteenth of November, the physicians again urged their refractory patient to take the medicines they prescribed, and were seconded by the prayers of the empress. lie repulsed them with some haughtiness, hut quickly repenting of his hastiness of temper, which in fact was one of the symptoms of the disease, he said, "Attend to me, Stcpliiegen, and you too, Sir Andrew Wyllie. I have much pleasure in seeing you, but you plague mc so often about your medicine, that really I must give up your company if you will talk of nothing else.'' He however was at last induced to take a dose of calomel. In the evening, the fever had made such fearful progress that it appeared necessary to call in a priest. Sir Andrew Wyllie, at the instance of the empress. entered the chamber of the dying prince, and approaching his bed with tears in his eyes, advised him "to call in the aid of the Most High, and not to refuse the assistance of religion as he had already done that of medicine." The emperor instantly gave his ron-

sc n t. Upon the fifteenth, at fi\e o'clock in the morning, a humble village priest approached the imperial bed to receive the confession of his expiring sovereign. " .M\ father, Hod must lie merciful to kings," were the first words the emperor addressed to the minister of religion ; "indeed they require it so much more than other men." In Ibis sentence all the trials and temptations of the despotic ruler of a great people þÿ his territorial ambition, his jealousy, his political ruses, his distrusts, and ovcr-confidcncics, seem to he briefly comprehended. Then, apparently perceiving some timidity in the spiritual confessor his destiny had provided for him, he added, " iMy father, treat mc like an erring man, not as an emperor." The priest drew near the bed, received the confession of Ins august penitent, and administered to bin) the last sacraments. Then having been informed of the emperor's pertinacity in rejecting medicine, lie urged him to give up this fatal obstinacy, remarking, "that he feared <»'od would consider it absolutely suicidal." His admonitions made a deep impression upon the mind of the prince, who recalled Sir Andrew Wyllie, and, giving him his hand, bade him do what he pleased with him. Wyllie took advantage of this absolute surrender, to apply twenty leeches to the head of the emperor, hut the application was too late, the burning fever continually increased and the sufferer was given over. The intelligence filled the dying chamber with weeping domestics, who tenderly
loved their master. (To be continued )

Editor, Sir! 1 have perused the communication from II þÿ and perceive that lie attempts to throw some ridicule 011 the expression of " Champs dc Mars," as imputed to C ; hut I would beg him 111 future to he more observant, and better acquainted with his subject. I advise him to read the St. Thomas Times again more carefully, when he will lind that those high sounding words did not originate with C, hut were simply quoted from that paper. In regard to what kind of a militia II would wish to establish, I cannot divine, þÿ he declares that after monthly trainings " the sight of one of the militia corps under drill gratifies his love of the ridiculous! and that to see 50 or 00 men marching in a straight line as the letter 8 up and down the parade ground þÿ is also ridiculous!" THE LAST DAYS OF THE EMPE- ROR ALEXANDER. ( Concluded from our last.) The empress still occupied her place | by the bed-side, which she had never press quitted but once, in order to allow her ! ance generally discovered in those subprivate to his confessor. She returned the fever of the country; the brain was to the post assigned her by conjugal tenderness directly the priest had quitted it. Two hours after he had made his peace with God, Alexander experienced more severe pain than he had yet felt ; " Kings," said he, " suffer more than others." He had called one of his at- | chamber was hung with black, and the tendants to listen to this remark, with the air of one communicating a secret. Tie stopped, and then as if recalling something he had forgotten, said in a whisper, "they have committed an intiimous action." What did he mean by those words? Was he suspicions that his days had been shortened by poison? or did lie allude, with the last accents lie uttered, to the barbarous assassination of the Emperor Paul ? Eternity can alone re- ; remained in the apartment. The emveal the secret thoughts of Alexander I. of Russia. During the night, the dying prince lost consciousness. At two o'clock in the morning, Count Diebitch came to the empress, to inform her that an old man, named Alcxandrowitz, had saved many Tartars in the same malady. A ray of hope entered the heart of the

Sir Andrew Wyllie ordered hiiu to be sought for with haste. This interval was passed by the empress in prayer, yet she still kept her eyes fixed npon those of her husband, watching with intense attention the beams of life and light fading in their unconscious gaze. At nine in the morning, the old man was brought into the imperial chamber almost by force. The rank of the patient, perhaps, inspiring him with some fear respecting the consequences that might follow his prescriptions, caused his extreme unwillingness. He approached the bed, looked at his dying sovereign, and shook his head. He was questioned respecting this doubtful sign. " It is too late to give him medicine ; besides, those 1 have cured were not sick of the same malady." With these words of the peasant physician, the last hopes of the empress \ anished ; but if pure and ardent prayers could have prevailed with God, Alexander would have been saved. On the sixteenth of November, according to the usual method of measuring time, but on the first of December, if we follow the Russian calendar, at fifty minutes after ten in the morning, Alexander Paulowitz, Emperor of all the Russias, expired. The historical career of the Emperor Vlexander is well known to every reader, but the minor matters of every-day life mark the man, while public details properly denote the sovereign. The faults of Alexander are comprised iri his infidelity to a beautiful, accomplished, and aflectionatc wife, lie respected her even while wounding her delicate feelings by his criminal attachments to other women. After many years of mental pain, the injured Elizabeth gave him the choice of giving her up, or banishing an imperious mistress, by whom the emperor had a numerous family- Alexander could not resolve to separate forever from his amiable and virtuous consort þÿ he made the sacrifice she required of him. His gallantry sometimes placed him m unprinccly situations, and brought hiiii in contact with persons immeasurably beneath him. lie once fell in love with a tailor's wife at Warsaw, and not being well acquainted with the character of the pretty grisette, construed her icceptaiiee of the visit he proposed making her, into approbation of his suit, ''he lair Pole was too simple, .and had been too virtuously brought up, to comprehend his intentions. Her husband was absent, so she thought it would not be proper to receive the imperial visit

alone ; she made, therefore, a re-union of her own and her husband's relations þÿ neb people of the bourgeoise class þÿ and when the emperor entered her saloon, he found himself in company with thirty or forty persons, to whom lie was immediately introduced by bis fair and innocent hostess. The astonished sovereign was obliged to make himself agreeable to the party, none ot whom appear to have divined his criminal intentions. He made no further attempt to corrupt the innocence of this beautiful woman, whose simplicity formed the safeguard of her virtue. \ severe trial separated him forever from Ins last mistress, who had borne liini a daughter ; litis child was the idol of Ins heart, and to form her mind was the pleasure of Ins life. At eighteen the young lady eclipsed every woman in his empire by her dazzling beauty and graceful maimers. Suddenly she was seized with an infectious fever, lor which uo physician in St. I'etcrsburgh could find a remedy. Her mother, selfish and timid, deserted the sick chamber ot the suft'ering girl, over whom the bitter tears of a father were vanity shed, while lie kept incessant vigils over one whom lie would have saved from the power of the grave at the expense of his life and empire. The dying daughter asked incessantly for her mother upon whose bosom she desired to breathe her last sigh, but neither the passionate entreaties nor the

<8 2i <D 1 A T 'i 3. commands of her imperial lover could induce the unnatural parent to risk her health by granting the interview for which her poor child craved, and she expired in the arms of her father, without the consolation of bidding her mother a last adieu. Some days after the death of his natural daughter, the Emperor Alexander entered the house of an English otlicer, to whom lie was much attached. He was in deep mourning, and appeared very unhappy. "I have just followed to the grave," lie said, " as a private person, the remains of my poor child, and I can not yet forgive the unnatural woman who deserted the death- bed of her daughter. Besides, my sin, which 1 never repented of, has found me out, and the vengeance of Hod has fallen upon its fruits. Ves, 1 deserted the best and most amiable of wives, the object of my first affection, for women who neither possessed her beauty nor merit. 1 have prefered to the empress even this unnatural mother, whom I now regard with loathing and horror. My wife shall never again have cause to reproach my broken faith. Devotion and bis strict adherence to bis promise, balmed the wound, which, however, only death could heal. To the secret agony which through life had haunted the bosom of the son was added that of the father, and the return of Alexander to the paths of virtue and religion originated in the loss of this beloved daughter, smitten, lie considered for bis sins. The friendship of this prince for Madame Krudener had nothing criminal in

its nature, though it furnished a theme doubt the purity of Platonic attachments between individuals of opposite sexes. In regard to this emperor's political career, full of ambition and stratagem, we can only re-echo bis dying words to bis confessor: "God must be mercilnl to kings!" His career, however, varied by losses on the field, or humiliated bv treaties, ended triumphantly with the laurels of war and the olives of peace ; and he bore to bis far northern empire the keys of Paris as a trophy of his arms. His moderation demands the praise of posterity, and excited the admiration of the French nation at large. His immoral conduct as a man and a husband was afterward effaced by bis sincere repentance, and lie died in the arms of the most faithful and atl'ectionate of wives, who could not long survive her irreparable loss. His death was deeply lamented by his subjects, who, if they did not enroll his name among the greatest of their rulers, never have hesitated to denote him as the best and most merciful sovereign who ever sat upon the Russian throne.

There is that in the following brief social homily which renders it worthy of a better preservation than an inscription upon an unappropriated slip of paper in the "Drawer;" "There is no better evidence of ill-breeding than the practice of interrupting another in conversation while speaking, or commencing a remark before another lias fully closed. No well-bred person ever does it, nor continues conversation long with a person who docs do it. The latter often finds an interesting conversation abruptly waived, closed, or declined by for scandal to those who are apt to i the former, without even suspecting the cause. A well-bred person will not even interrupt one who is in all respects greatly his inferior. If you wish to judge the good-breeding of a person with whom yon are but little acquainted, observe him, or her, strictly in this respect, and you will not be deceived. þÿ However intelligent, fluent, or easy one may appear, this practice proves the absence of true politeness. It is often amusing to see persons, priding themselves on the gentility of their manners, and pear putting forth all in their efforts to advantage many other to ap- respects, so readily betray all "in this particular.
