From, the St. Thomas Times, Aug. 20, 1851. On Monday last we were visited by a severe gale from the Worth East. About 10 þÿo clock on Sunday night the wind began to freshen, and continued steady until the next morning, when it increased in violence, causing much alarm to the inhabitants. It will be remembered that the memorable gale of 1837 occurred in the month of August ; this circumstance tended greatly to increase the fears of the community, particularly when it was discovered that the Barometer had fallen several degrees. At an early hour the merchants generally had their establishments closed, and inthe qui rire to secure iheir dwellings. þÿ early the Monday deed all the St. Thomas folk were on Some families were compelled to leave their homes and seek more secure shelter abroad. The sea rose with considerable fury, and washed away many of the wharves and other little appurtenances. weather the storm, and þÿ The vessels in port did their best to best þÿbowers able nature. were in requisition. The lloyal Mail Steamer Dee rode out the gale þÿ like a duck on the þÿwater, and the Merlin also behaved admirably ; but we were sorry to notice the Derurnt in rather a precarious situation. She was moored alongside the þÿCompany wharf, s and in consequence of two square rigged vessels lying right ahead of her, she could not by any possibility have left her moorings in rase of need without the certainty of running into one or other of them. Happily however she had no occasion to put to sea. The American brig Wanderer

was driven ashore, and received but little damage considering the fury of the gale. This vessel will likely be hauled up on the Marine Slip undergo to repairs. It is estimated that her repairs before she can be ready for sea will cost about $ ,000. 1 A Dominican brigantine also left her moorings, and in consequence of being very light of ballast, she was turned bottom up. The amount of injury which she has sustained is not yet ascertained. Connected with these particulars it is our melancholy of duty notice the death by drowning three to persons. A boat with one man and two women was upset whilst coming across from the þÿ careening þÿhole, and her passengers met with a watery grave. We have not heard of any more loss of life. The damage to property on shore has been trivial. Several wooden fences were blown down, a few tiles and slates uplifted from the and roofs houses in town, a few trees destroy- of one or two ed. Some slight injury has also attended lately erected, the Episcopal Church. The railings and parapet walls have suffered. The greatest anxiety prevailed to watch the change of the weather at meridian, but at this time no favorable symptoms were perceptible. About 3 p. m., however the Barometer began to rise, as also the spirits of the good people, when it was apparent that the wind had abated ; and by midnight the scene was changed from a storm to a calm. VVe have much cause to be thankful for our preservation on this occasion, for had the wind but changed, serious

consequences may have ensued. IVo inthe country districts, telligence whatever has but reached us from we trust our rural friends have been as fortunate as ourselves. This blow must have been experienced by the sister colonies ot Saint Croix anil Saint þÿJohn s, and also to Windward þÿ including the British \ irgin Islands þÿ and we are anxious to receive accounts. To-day the weather is line ; in fact it has been so since yestermorn, and we humble ourselves before an All-wise Providence for a continuance of His gracious mercies.

In the year of Grace 151, the Dan;- !i Colonies bid fair to enter their apprenticeship to the Art ot Legislative Government ; whether it will be necessary to fix the term of Indenture at three, Jive or seven years, will rest in a great degree on the aptitude of the indented. Certainly the conditions of the Indenture are pretty rigid, admit of little license or scope to the Apprentice ; but the old saying, þÿ a sharp master makes a good þÿworkman, may hereafter be productive of good fruit, and compensate the hard-fated Apprentice for the severity and rigidness of the rules by which he is bound. And the more inconvenient and prescribed the rules, the greater credit will be due to him who by patient application and perseverance ultimately perfects his task þÿ þÿ Tis not for mortals to command success, but we will deserve þÿit. þÿ lb. A public journalist will not on all occasions obtrude lus individual opinion on subjects in general ; but in the presence of the organic reforms about to take place, the public weal demands that his voice should now be heard in the discussion, advocacy or defence of such reforms þÿ explaining their merits, and pointing out to the parties concerned, or recipients, the important modifications not only necessary but unavoidable to afford every facility to their operations. The commissioners will without loss of time furnish their report on the Colonial Law graciously proposed by llis Majesty for the government of the Danish West India Islands. We therefore feel it our duty to refer to certain paragraphs, and to solicit the particular attention of the parties whose recommendations will be the means of effecting the amendments or modifications, indispensable to secure their efficiency and adaptation to the present wants of the inhabitants. Amendments : 1st Paragraph. þÿ That the Colonial Assembly be invested with a full deliberative voice with regard to the exercise of the Legislative power. 4th Paragraph. We recommend a thor- þÿ ough revision of this paragraph, and particularly that portion which alludes to the Special Ordinances

relating to schools and public instruction, the abrogation of the regulations between employers and labourers, masters and servants þÿ the support of the poor, and the þÿ militia. (ith Paragraph. þÿ That the Assembly be empowered receive the petitions to of private individuals, and thereby be the medium for the conveyance of said documents (on which they will express their opinions) 1o the Governor, that the same may lie laid before the king, or the Home Authorities. 9th Paragraph. þÿ The members to be elected to serve three instead of six years. 1 Ot h Paragraph. þÿ A modification extending the right of Eranchisc to every freeholder, male or female as well as Burghers. The public will disagree on the propriety of admit ting /i malts as voters, but in the English Islam's females enjoy this privilege. 18th Paragraph. þÿ We recommend that the Commissioners endeavour to establish the þÿ þÿBallot. 23rd Paragraph. þÿ That the Assembly Inconvened to meet in general session semi-annually, for the dispatch of public business; and whenever dissolved by the Governor, «n such an emergency a new \\ l it to be issued forthwith for the election of new members to form an Assembly, so organized as to be able to hold their session at the ordinary term. 25th Paragraph. þÿ The records of the proceedings of the Assembly to be kept in Danish and English , and the sittings of that Body to be public. These are the important amendments we deem necessary to impart vitality and efficiency to Laws having for their
object the well being of the inhabitants, and tbe prosperity of the Danish Colonies. þÿ lb.

Prom the St. Lucia Palladium, Aug. 8. Volcanic Eruption in lite Island of Martinique. WV have just received Martinique letters of the 6th instant. They bring the startling accounts of a frightlul eruption of the long dormant volcano ot the Pelee Mountain at that Island, which took place during the night of Tuesday last the 5th instant. Like the great and memorable eruption of the St. Vincent Soufriere in 1812, the phenomenon at Martinique is described with a " noise as having been simimr to accompanied of the approach thunder, still nearer and nearer, with a vibration that affected 'lie feelings and hearing." It appears, however, that, beyond a layer ot grey sand, gritty particles of calcined earth, and favilla, found in the morning upon the streets, houses, and shipping, as having been thrown forth by the volcano in the night, the people of St. Pierre were, up i to our last accounts, uninformed of the effects of the phenomenon. The following extract of a private letter may, in the absence ot more collected parMculars, give some idea ot the eruption : þÿ " St. Pierre, Clh August lbol. v hicti "illumed irom about midnight to four o'clock A string rumbling noise was heard last night, . this morning. At daylight this morning, we observed 'bree streaming chimneys of smoke on the 1 elee lountain. One of these was of black smoke, resembling the smoke from a steamship, though ten times more voluminous than the chimney of our steam-fri- "ate. The other two were formed of a whitish smoke. 1 assure you I never before saw anything so grand.

The town is all covered over with grey ashes. A 'reat many |tersons have gone to the Mount, but cannot reach it before night. There has been no shock of earthquake felt ; hut persons living in the neighbourhood declare that they were driven from their homes by the strong smell of sulphur, and ' the tear of danger from their vicinity to the eruption. Another letter of the same date, says: " We had during the night an eruption of the volcano on Mount l'elee. The whole town, as far as the covered Mouillage, as well as all the surrounding country, I're- over with ashes. The population of is chcur had to fly their homes during the night and come the whole way to St. Pierre. As for my family, it was not until rising this morning, we heard of the occurrence, there not having been, thank God, any earthquake. It is not possible as yet to give you any particulars of this phenomenon or of its effects , on shall soon have them in the journals. It may, however, he inferred tiiat no calamitous result has i risen from it, for, had there been any, we should have known by this time. The l'elec Mountain, which is the highest land in Martinique, stands at the north of the island, and, according to the map published by royal authority in 1831 is represented as bearing an altitudc'of of the sea. 4,438 English feet from mountain It is from this the level chiefly that the numerous springs issue although strikingly by which the island characterised is watered ; and, with the indelible marks of an ancient volcano,
we do not remember to have ever fallen in with the record of any of its eruptions. It is to be hoped that amongst those

<0 » ®1 A T 11 3 inhabitants stated to have been attracted to the site of the volcano by its recent eruption, some scientific explorer will be found to enlighten us with the result of his observations on so interesting a phenomenon. There is said to he an identity of origin in þÿ tions a connection earthquakes and or more volcanic erup- less intimate in the agency of the one with the other. In the case of Etna and Vesuvius, it is recorded, they rarely return to a state of activity after an interval of repose without some antecedent earthquake, the latter usually ceasing so soon as the volcano has once established lor itselt a vent whereby the elastic vapours we can discharge themselves. So, too, which have seen, that the earthquake destroyed Caracas in 1812, at (he same time that the shores of the Mississippi were in sympathetic commotion, was followed in eight days by the memorable eruption of the Soufriere in St. Vincent. May it not, then, he hoped, that the awful oscillations of the earth, almost continuously in action during the last two months at the neighbouring island of Guadaloupe will now be at ail end?

The Correo dc Caracas announces that the Steamer Bertha Harrassowitz, of 400 tons, and 150 horse-power, lias been built at Baltimore, intended as a Packet to ply on the coast of the Republic þÿ The contract entered into by the Gov eminent and Messrs. Harrassowitz A Co., stipulates that the said Steamer, conjointly with the Graciosa, will convey the official as well as private correspondence from Cumana to Maracayho. The Contractors will receive the amount which is at the present moment charged by the General Post Office. The Steamer will also receive the European mails at St. Thomas, and on her return call at Porto Rico and Curasao. This new arrangement oil'ers great advantages to the mercantile community and the public in general. From the statements which are published in the American papers, no expense has been spared to render the Bertha Harrassowitz a vessel of great speed, and possessing all the comforts for the accommodation of passengers. The enterprising projectors are worthy of support, whilst our neighbours will have the facilities to perform a voyage to the United States in 9 days, connected as the Venezuelan Steamer will he with the Merlin Steamer, running betwecn New York and St. Thomas. þÿ Messrs. Harrassowitz &, Co., intend to form an arrangement with the Directors of the Steamers between Southampton and St. Thomas, which will afford additional benefits to La Guaira and other Venezuelan ports.

From the Illustrated London News. Launch ol' the " Amazon. » This vessel, the largest timber-built steam-ship ever constructed in England, was launched on Saturday from the shipyard of the Messrs Green, at Blackwall.

The Amazon is one of the fleet of new vessels about to be placed by the Royal Mail Steam-Packet Company on the West India service, the steamers at present employed upon that station being found not sufficiently powerful to maintain that degree of speed and regularity which is required by the increased demand for more rapid communication with our West Indian colonies. The Amazon is a ship of 2256 tons burden. Her entire length is 300 feet, and her breadth 41 feet. The whole period occupied in her construction has been little more than nine months; and in about a year from the time that her keel was laid down this noble vessel will have been fully completed, and ready to proceed on her first voyage. Iler motive force will consist of two engines of 1600 horse-power, which are to be supplied by Messrs. Seaward and Capel. A large and fashionable company, including several foreigners of distinction, was invited by the directors of the Royal Mail Steam-packet Company to be present on Saturday at the interesting spectacle of the launch, and the river in front of the ship-yard was crowded with small crafts, containing numerous visitors from London. Shortly after one o'clock, the signal was given for removing the supports ; and after the busy operation of 1 he shipwrights' hammers for a few minutes, the enormous vessel glided with an easy graceful motion into her native element amidst the cheers of the spectators, receiving at the same time from Lady A. Paget the title of the Amazon ,

according to the customary form. She was immediately taken in tow by a couple of river steamers, and brought to moorings a little above Messrs: Green's yard. The friends of the Directors of the Company were afterwards received at a hospitable entertainment in the spacious cabins of the Trafalgar, which was lying in an adjacent dock.

The clocks in all the church towers struck; scarcely a single house remains uninjured, numerous chimneys fell in, and the furniture and utensils in the rooms were overthrown, and broken. þÿ

Paris, Wednesday Morning. þÿ Yesterday, after the reading of M. de Torqueville's report, on the revision of the Constitution, M. de Melon read his report on tlie petitions addressed to the Assembly, on the same subject. In this latter report, the inferior authorities are blamed tor the part they took in getting up the petitions, but it is admitted that, on ttie part of the minister of the Interior, nothing was done which can be considereu illegal or an abuse of power. The debate on the revision of the Constitution is iixed for the 14tii instant. þÿ Thirty Members nave inscribed their names as intending to speak in favour of the revision, the most important of whom are MM. de Falloux, Odillon Barrot, de Broglie, Bauchart, de Montalembert, de Kerdrel, de Riancy, de Melon. LOU BAR MY. The Progresso, of the oth inst., announces that the Military Commander of Lodi had been stabbed with a poniard. A letter trom Venice, published by The Genoa Gazette , of the 4th inst., states that fifteen respectable inhabitants of Troviso had been arrested and thrown into prison. Among them were several clergymen and physicians, a merchant, and two ladies. They were, it appears, accused of having subscribed to the Muzzini loan.

THE PAPAL STATES. We read in The Milan Gazette, under date of Rome, 30th ult., that a man, armed with a stiletto, was found concealed the day before, in the house of Colonel Nardoni, with the intention, no doubt, of attempting his assassination. The new bank of the Pontiticial States commenced its operations on the 1st of July. SWITZERLAND. The Federal Council of Switzerland has drawn up a decree for the execution of the railways proposed by 31 r. Stephenson. One line is to traverse the country from the Lake of Constance to Geneva, passing by Zurich. A branch line is to run from this trunk line to the Basle Railway to unite with the German and French lines. Another line is to proceed from the Lake of Constance to Coire, in the Grisons, to be prolonged afterwards across the Alps, by Luckmanicr into Lombardy. The total length of these lines is to be 650 kilometres (4061 English miles), and the expense 102,123,000f., or 137.1 12f. per kilometre.

The Female Street Orderlies. þÿ We know of none, among the numerous acts of utility performed by ladies in the present day, involving so much self-sacrifice as the practice adopted by our fashionably-dressed women, of cleansing the public thoroughfares. The length to which the fair sex go in the article ol dress, is only to be exceeded by the lengths to which they go in rendering their dresses useful to the whole community. Few who have not watched the elegantly-habited female pedestrian passing through thick and thin, to assist in sweeping the London streets, can form any idea of what she carries in her train when she sets the example we have alluded to. All that is required to render the ladies efficient and constant scavengers of the metropolitan foot pavements, is to organise them into a body of female orderlies, and, though the City Court of Sewers rejected 31r Cochrane's proposition to cleanse the streets hy means of his troop, the objection being founded chietly on the class to which its members belong, we have little doubt that the services of the ladies, should they he tendered, would he accepted with eagerness. Since the commencement of the shilling days has admitted to the Crystal Palace a majority of those belonging to a class who are self-interested enough to study economy and personal cleanliness, the building gets only, on Saturdays, the benefit of that thorough sweeping which the five shilling classes are prepared to administer at the sacrifice of their dresses, and

at the cost of accumulating about themselves all the dust and dirt that wouid otherwise remain on the floor of the Exhibition. Unfortunately, the fine-lady scavengers are chiefly among those who consider the payment of five shillings necessary to protect the in from the con tact of the vulgar ; and they do not, therefore, attend in large numbers on the shilling days; so that the only way to secure their scavenging services would be to have a second five shilling day, when, released from the fear of all association with what some of them would call the scum of the earth, they might take away all the dust and dirt of the ground on their legs and petticoats. þÿ Punch.
